idiom_name: std::weak_ptr<T> + lock() (C++11): non-owning companion of std::shared_ptr
implementation_notes: C++ has the pattern in the standard library at value level: std::weak_ptr holds a non-owning reference to an object managed by std::shared_ptr and is converted to a strong reference with lock(), which is atomic and returns an empty shared_ptr instead of throwing (the shared_ptr constructor from a weak_ptr throws std::bad_weak_ptr). The canonical uses are breaking a shared_ptr cycle by making one edge weak and keeping weak handles in registries or caches that promote on lookup; std::enable_shared_from_this and its weak_from_this() let an object hand out weak references to itself. The implementation is not hand-written - the control block carries a separate weak count, so the allocation survives while any weak_ptr remains, but the managed object is destroyed as soon as the last strong owner goes.
code_sketch:
std::shared_ptr<Session> s = Session::open(addr);   // strong owner
std::weak_ptr<Session> watch = s;                   // registry/cache edge
if (auto locked = watch.lock())                     // atomic promotion
    locked->round_trip();                           // strong for the duration
// s.reset(): the object dies; watch.expired() becomes true
pitfalls: The managed object may be destroyed while weak_ptr instances still exist, and the allocation is not freed until the last weak_ptr is gone: a long-lived registry of weak_ptrs keeps storage, not the object, alive.
weak_ptr has no accessor - every use must go through lock() (or the throwing shared_ptr constructor); calling expired() and then dereferencing a raw pointer obtained elsewhere re-introduces the race.
An object can only be weakly referenced through shared_ptr ownership: a stack object or a unique_ptr target cannot be watched, so adopting weak_ptr means adopting shared ownership for that class.

variants.name: QPointer<T> guarded pointer for QObject subclasses
variants.idiom_name: QPointer<T> (Qt 5/6) - a guarded pointer cleared by the QObject destructor
variants.implementation_notes: The Qt realization watches objects that are not managed by a shared_ptr: QPointer<T> behaves like a normal T* except that it is automatically cleared to nullptr when the referenced object is destroyed, so T must derive from QObject and ownership stays whatever the QObject parent/child tree or the application already does. Reach for it when the target is a widget, controller or service whose lifetime the framework manages and shared ownership would be artificial; when shared ownership does exist, Qt's QSharedPointer/QWeakPointer pair mirrors the standard-library design instead.
pitfalls: QPointer only tracks QObject-derived types, and it is cleared by the QObject destructor: a QPointer to a widget is not cleared before that widget's children are destroyed (documented Qt behaviour).
QPointer is not thread-safe - QObject has thread affinity, so the guarded pointer must be used from the object's thread, unlike std::weak_ptr's atomic lock().

variants.name: Boost.SmartPtr weak_ptr (pre-C++11 legacy)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11 the same design shipped as Boost.SmartPtr: boost::weak_ptr stores a weak reference to an object owned by boost::shared_ptr and promotes it with lock(), which returns an empty shared_ptr instead of throwing boost::bad_weak_ptr. This is the ancestor the standard adopted, so it remains the realization to recognise in codebases that predate C++11; new code should use std::weak_ptr unless the project is pinned to a pre-C++11 toolchain and Boost is already part of the stack.
pitfalls: boost::weak_ptr only works with boost::shared_ptr: mixing boost and std smart pointers on one object creates two control blocks and undefined behaviour.
The interface matches the standard one, which makes migration easy, but boost::shared_ptr predates the standard ABI and cannot cross library boundaries that expect std::shared_ptr.
